subtopic: A conflict between two team members
subtype: Approach: emotion-aware timing of the discussion [Thinking]
passage: Note from Uday, engineering director. On Monday Manjula stopped by my desk. Two of her people, Tanmay and Divya, had been snapping at each other all week. Manjula wanted to sort it out, but said, "They're both running on empty until Thursday's launch. If I bring it up now, it lands as one more problem." So she waited. The launch went out on Thursday evening. On Friday afternoon Manjula took the two of them to a quiet corner with coffee. I walked past twice: voices low, and at one point a laugh. By Monday Manjula told me they had agreed who reviews what. All I did was leave them alone and approve a half-day for the team.

qa.q: When did Manjula meet Tanmay and Divya to talk?
qa.a: Manjula took them to a quiet corner on Friday afternoon.

qa.q: Why did Manjula wait before raising the problem, and what was she worried about?
qa.a: Manjula worried that Tanmay and Divya were too exhausted before launch, and that raising it then would feel like one more problem.

qa.q: What else could Manjula do to keep the peace, and why?
qa.a: Manjula could check in with each of them a week later, because a calm talk may still need a follow-up to settle into habit.

qa.q: How might Divya have felt about the timing of the talk?
qa.a: Divya probably felt relieved and more open, since the pressure of the launch was over and there was space to speak calmly.

grounding: Illustrates a lead seeing that two colleagues are stressed by a release and waiting until the day after launch to talk, when the discussion is calm.

subtopic: A conflict between two team members
subtype: Approach: escalating to HR for a serious conduct issue [Revision]
passage: Afreen, you asked when to stop mediating. I'm Jasleen. I was a young woman, a first-time lead, with two colleagues at odds. I began as usual, sitting with each one alone. The first talked about deadlines. The second, in a low voice, told me the first had made remarks about their accent and said they would never make a proper engineer. That was not a quarrel over tasks. My stomach sank, because a joint meeting would put the second person in a room with the person who said those things. I wrote down the dates and the words as they were told, added nothing, told the second colleague it was not their fault and what I would do, and took my notes to HR that afternoon. The company's process took over. My job was to support the team and keep the record straight.

qa.q: Where did Jasleen take the notes?
qa.a: Jasleen took the notes to HR that afternoon.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel on hearing what the second colleague said?
qa.a: Jasleen's stomach sank, because a joint meeting could put the second colleague in the room with the person who made the remarks.

qa.q: At which point in the story did Jasleen change approach, and why?
qa.a: Jasleen changed approach when the second colleague described demeaning remarks rather than a task dispute, because mediation was not enough for a conduct issue.

qa.q: How might the second colleague have felt on telling Jasleen?
qa.a: The second colleague was probably afraid and vulnerable but relieved to be listened to and told it was not their fault.

grounding: Illustrates a lead seeing that demeaning remarks are beyond mediation, documenting the facts and bringing in HR under company process.

subtopic: A conflict between two team members
subtype: Approach: follow-up check-ins and adjusting the arrangement [Revision]
passage: Two weeks after the new handover rules began, Avni booked ten minutes with each of the two in the glass meeting room. Sonali went first. "The rules help, but the note takes me forty minutes and nobody reads to the end." Then Vishal said the same thing in different words: too long. Avni looked at the template on the screen. It had nine headings. Together they cut it down to three: changed, pending, contact. Both nodded. "I'll ask again next month," Avni said, and put a fifteen-minute slot in the calendar for the first Friday of each month. Sonali left the room looking lighter, and Vishal was already opening the shorter template.

qa.q: How many headings did the template have?
qa.a: The template had nine headings.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel on leaving the meeting room?
qa.a: Sonali felt lighter and relieved, since the note would no longer take forty minutes.

qa.q: What else could Avni do at the monthly check-in, and why?
qa.a: Avni could ask whether anyone reads the shortened notes and change the format again if not, because a rule should be adjusted until it serves the people using it.

qa.q: How might Vishal have seen the two-week check-in?
qa.a: Vishal probably felt listened to and glad the complaint led to a quick change, since Vishal was already opening the shorter template.

grounding: Illustrates a lead checking after two weeks how new working rules are going, shortening a too-long handover note and keeping a short monthly check-in.

subtopic: A conflict between two team members
subtype: Approach: reassigning work to reduce contact temporarily [Revision]
passage: Two long talks had not worked. Kiran and Prakash still spoke to each other through curt, cold ticket comments, and the release was three weeks away. Ankita opened the sprint board and drew a line down the middle. Kiran took the search module and Prakash took checkout. The only connection was a small interface: five fields in, five fields out, written on one page that both signed off. "It isn't forever," Ankita told each of them separately. "Only this sprint, so the work doesn't stall while things cool down." In stand-up the two hardly looked at each other, but the tickets moved. At the end of the sprint, Ankita paired them again on one small task.

qa.q: How many fields does the interface pass in and out?
qa.a: The interface has five fields in and five fields out.

qa.q: What does the way Kiran and Prakash hardly looked at each other in stand-up suggest?
qa.a: It suggests they were still tense and cold with each other, even though the work was moving.

qa.q: What else could Ankita do before rejoining them, and why?
qa.a: Ankita could check with each of them privately whether they feel ready, because rejoining too early could bring the tension straight back.

qa.q: How might Prakash have felt about being moved to checkout?
qa.a: Prakash may have felt some relief at having space, and possibly a sting at being separated, as Ankita said it was not forever.

grounding: Illustrates a lead putting two colleagues on separate modules with a clean interface for a sprint so work continues while tension cools.

subtype: Approach: working backward from promotion criteria [Thinking]
passage: On the analytics floor, Aadhya printed the senior analyst criteria and laid them beside her own record on the desk. Ticked: technical depth, quality of reports, clear writing. Blank: cross-team ownership. "Working backwards," she said to Tejas, the colleague at the next desk. "They want someone who has run something across teams. I haven't." She looked at the calendar. The promotion cycle was two quarters away. She wrote a plan: propose a shared dashboard for sales and operations in the first quarter, lead the working group in the second, and collect feedback from both teams. Tejas raised an eyebrow. "That's a real project." "That's the point," Aadhya said.

qa.q: What was left blank on Aadhya's criteria sheet?
qa.a: Cross-team ownership was left blank.

qa.q: What did Aadhya realise while comparing the criteria with her record?
qa.a: Aadhya realised she lacked the cross-team experience the criteria ask for, and felt determined to build it.

qa.q: What else could Aadhya do to strengthen the plan, and why?
qa.a: Aadhya could ask her manager to confirm that the dashboard project counts as cross-team ownership, because agreement early avoids surprises at review.

qa.q: How might Tejas see Aadhya's plan?
qa.a: Tejas probably sees it as ambitious but real, since a raised eyebrow and the remark that it is a real project suggest respect.

grounding: Illustrates an analyst reading the senior criteria, seeing a gap in cross-team ownership and planning a project over two quarters to build that evidence.

subtype: Approach: asking the manager for explicit expectations [Action]
passage: With appraisal season six weeks away and his manager Urmila about to leave on a work trip, Chaitanya caught her at the pantry. "Can I take ten minutes tomorrow? I want to ask what a promotion would need, and by when." She looked surprised, then nodded. The next morning she named three gaps: presenting to senior people, mentoring a junior, and owning a project from start to finish. "By the September review." He wrote them down and read them back to check. "Could we look at progress once a month?" Urmila put a recurring slot on both calendars before she left for the airport, and Chaitanya walked back to his desk feeling both nervous and steadier.

qa.q: What three gaps did Urmila name?
qa.a: Urmila named presenting to senior people, mentoring a junior, and owning a project from start to finish.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel after the conversation?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt both nervous and steadier.

qa.q: What else could Chaitanya do to work on the gaps, and why?
qa.a: Chaitanya could pick one small chance this month to present to seniors, because early practice shows progress at the monthly reviews.

qa.q: How might Urmila have felt when asked so directly?
qa.a: Urmila was probably surprised at first and then pleased, since Chaitanya's clear question made it easy to set expectations.

grounding: Illustrates asking the manager directly what a promotion requires and by when, getting three named gaps and agreeing on monthly reviews.

subtype: Approach: keeping a running record of achievements [Action]
passage:
Looking back, the thing that changed my review was a plain file. The year before, I could barely remember what I'd done between January and June. So on the last day of every month I started a note: what I delivered, numbers if I had them, and any kind words. March: the invoice report that saved the finance team forty hours. April: a thank-you line from Naveen, my manager, about the client demo. When review season came and Naveen asked, "What have you achieved this year?", I didn't have to search my memory. I scrolled through the note and read out six items. It took ten minutes and felt like a conversation about facts, not about how well I recalled the year. I still write it every month.

Maria

qa.q: How many items did Maria read out in the review?
qa.a: Maria read out six items.

qa.q: How did Maria feel in the review after keeping the note?
qa.a: Maria felt calm and prepared, since there was no need to search memory.

qa.q: What else could Maria add to the note, and why?
qa.a: Maria could add a line on what was learned each month, because it shows growth as well as results.

qa.q: How might Naveen have found the review conversation?
qa.a: Naveen probably found it easier and clearer, since specific facts gave the discussion something solid to talk about.

grounding: Illustrates keeping a monthly note of delivered work, numbers and feedback so review conversations are concrete rather than memory based.

subtype: Approach: seeking a sponsor beyond the immediate manager [Thinking]
passage:
Subject: Could you mentor me?

Dear Irawati,

I've learned that promotions here get decided by a committee, and my manager is only one voice in it. I realised I'd like someone in that room who has seen my work first-hand. Your team's roadmap overlaps with mine, and I've admired the way you run your reviews. Would you be willing to meet once a month for half an hour? I could share my planning documents and invite you to my demo on the 18th, so you can see the work and judge it for yourself. I know your calendar is full, and I'd be grateful for whatever time you can spare.

Warm regards,
Bhaskar

qa.q: Who decides promotions, according to Bhaskar?
qa.a: Promotions here get decided by a committee.

qa.q: What is Bhaskar worried about, judging from the email?
qa.a: Bhaskar is worried about being unseen by the people deciding, since the manager is only one voice in the committee.

qa.q: What else could Bhaskar do to build support, and why?
qa.a: Bhaskar could also share progress with the manager so both know the plan, because a manager and a sponsor working together strengthen the case.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel on receiving this email?
qa.a: Irawati may feel flattered and cautious about time, but the small, specific request and the invitation to the demo make it easier to say yes.

grounding: Illustrates realising that a committee decides promotions and asking a senior leader in another team to mentor and see one's work so someone speaks for the writer.

subtype: Approach: waiting to be noticed for hard work [Pitfall]
passage: Sushma had worked past nine on most nights for two years. She assumed the committee would notice, and so she never mentioned that she wanted a bigger role. Her manager thought of her as dependable, the one who fixed things quietly. When the promotion committee met, with only one slot in the year's budget, her manager described her as reliable and could not say what bigger role she was ready for. Arnab, who had asked in March what the next level needed and led one small project, was promoted. Sushma heard it at the tea counter and smiled, then went back to her desk and stared at the screen without typing.

qa.q: How late did Sushma work on most nights?
qa.a: Sushma worked past nine on most nights.

qa.q: How was Sushma feeling at the tea counter?
qa.a: Sushma was hurt and deflated, though she smiled, and afterwards she stared at the screen without typing.

qa.q: What could Sushma do next, and why?
qa.a: Sushma could tell her manager she wants a bigger role and ask what it takes, because the committee can only weigh a case that someone has made.

qa.q: How might Sushma's manager have seen her at the committee?
qa.a: The manager saw a reliable person but had no goal or bigger-role evidence to present, so there was nothing to argue for.

grounding: Illustrates assuming long hours will speak for themselves and never discussing a goal, so the committee sees reliability but no case and a colleague who asked is promoted.

passage: Anand said yes to everything that carried the director's name: the launch deck, the town-hall demo, the client dashboard, the hackathon team. In his Mumbai office his calendar looked like a bus timetable. By week six he had missed the deadline on the dashboard, and then the next one, on a quarterly report. Samir, across from him at lunch, said gently, "You're on eleven things." Anand shrugged. "Visibility matters." At the review, his manager laid the list on the table: eleven activities, two late, none finished with real depth. "It looks scattered," the manager said. Anand went home wondering whether being seen and being trusted with a big goal were really the same thing.

qa.q: How many things was Anand working on?
qa.a: Anand was working on eleven things.

qa.q: How did Anand feel when Samir mentioned the eleven things?
qa.a: Anand felt defensive, shrugging it off by saying visibility matters, before the review left him unsettled.

qa.q: What could Anand do instead of taking every high-profile task, and why?
qa.a: Anand could choose two or three tasks that matter most and finish them well, because a few clear results make a stronger record than many half-done ones.

qa.q: How might Samir have felt watching Anand's schedule fill up?
qa.a: Samir was probably concerned for Anand, which is why Samir raised it gently over lunch.

grounding: Illustrates taking on every high-profile task, spreading thin and missing deadlines, so the many activities look scattered rather than strong.
